source.title: Layer-Aware Representation Filtering: Purifying Finetuning Data to Preserve LLM Safety Alignment
source.authors: Hao Li; Lijun Li; Zhenghao Lu; Xian Wei; Rui Li; Jing Shao; Lei Sha

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites refusal-direction work and uses intermediate representations to rank fine-tuning data, but does not test the claimed difference-in-means direction by removing or adding it.
record.gate_note: The paper reports whole-layer parameter scaling and refusal-count sensitivity to identify safety-sensitive layers. These are not tests of the claimed single direction, so the results are recorded as none-version findings. The many ASR results for data-selection and fine-tuning methods are not results about that direction or its specified interventions.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Arditi et al. as motivation and uses a safe-minus-unsafe response representation difference (at a layer chosen by whole-layer parameter scaling) to rank fine-tuning data. It never builds the harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction, never ablates or adds it, and reports only its own data-selection method's ASR against baselines. The layer-scaling results measure refusal sensitivity to whole-layer weight scaling, not a direction.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Benign fine-tuning data contain safety-degrading samples. LARF identifies them efficiently via layer-specific representation similarity, and removing them mitigates safety degradation without harming utility.
record.recipe_differences: LARF selects data using similarity to safe and unsafe reference representations at a layer chosen by whole-layer scaling sensitivity. It does not use the original harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction or its ablation/addition intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The selected safety-sensitive layer differs by model. Layer sensitivity is evaluated using α∈{0.1, 0.2} on an overrejection dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling a single mid layer's attention and FFN weights by 1±α shifts refusal counts on an overrejection set sharply. The most sensitive layer differs by model: 13 for Llama3/3.1, 18 for Qwen2.5, 25 for Qwen2, 16 for Mistral, 21 for Phi-3-mini.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal behaviour is disproportionately sensitive to whole-layer weight scaling at a specific mid-depth 'safety layer'.

fits_no_version.finding: Benign fine-tuning samples whose representations at that layer lie closer to unsafe than to safe reference completions raise ASR the most after fine-tuning (e.g. Llama3.1 HarmBench 3.5% to 39%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety degradation from benign fine-tuning can be predicted by representational similarity to unsafe completions at a safety-sensitive layer.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The reported refusal-sensitivity intervention scales whole layers rather than isolating the claimed direction. No uncertainty estimates are given for these sensitivity results, and the overrejection calibration set has 110 instructions.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable. The remaining fine-tuning ASR, utility, and filtering comparisons concern LARF's data-selection method, not the claimed direction or its predicted interventions.

untested.parts: Difference-in-means direction is not constructed; no ablation or addition; no capability check of such an intervention.
No analysis of jailbreaks suppressing the direction. Fine-tuning degradation is not linked to the direction; the only link is PCA drift at a layer.
Effective-rank analysis of a transformation matrix is reported, but not as a test of refusal dimensionality.

record.verdict_notes: The paper calls its unsafe-minus-safe reference difference a 'rejection direction', but it is computed from completions, not instructions. It is used only for similarity scoring and is never intervened on, so it does not bear on V1. The rows are layer-selection values for the authors' method.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not construct the claimed harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction, ablate or add it, or measure effects on harmful and harmless requests and general capability.
No weight edit that removes the claimed direction from released models is tested.
The paper does not test whether attacks suppress the claimed direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
No affine, cone, or multiple-direction account of refusal is evaluated.
The paper does not separate harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer of the claimed direction is tested.
The paper does not test how refusal training choices determine whether the claimed direction exists.
Reasoning models are not evaluated for the claimed direction.

rows.subject: Llama3
rows.operation_detail: Scaled each layer's attention and feed-forward parameters by 1±α to measure changes in refusal responses; reported the maximum normalized change rate.
rows.measure: Maximum normalized refusal-count change rate k
rows.value: k = 370; the text says weakening layer 13 sharply reduces refusal responses and strengthening it sharply increases them.
rows.note: This perturbs whole-layer parameters, not the claimed single direction. The reported effect is on the overrejection dataset.
rows.check: Whole-layer attention/FFN weight scaling on a 110-item overrejection set. This is not an intervention on the refusal direction. It is also a layer-selection value for the authors' method, not a test of the claim. The row is otherwise accurate (k=370, layer 13).
